title: Diet and the evolution of human amylase gene copy number variation
authors: Perry GH, Dominy NJ, Claw KG, Lee AS, Fiegler H, Redon R, et al.
population: Populations with high-starch diets (50 European-Americans, 45 Japanese, 38 Hadza) and low-starch diets (36 Biaka, 15 Mbuti, 17 Datog, 25 Yakut)
funder: L.S.B. Leakey Foundation and Wenner-Gren Foundation (to N.J.D.), Department of Pathology, Brigham & Women's Hospital (to C.L.), National Institutes of Health (to the University of Louisiana at Lafayette New Iberia Research Center; RR015087, RR014491, RR016483) and the Wellcome Trust (H.F., R.R., N.P.C.).
result: Diploid copy number of the salivary amylase gene AMY1 correlated positively with salivary amylase protein in 50 European-Americans (P < 0.001; R2 = 0.351). At least 6 AMY1 copies were found in 70% of individuals from the combined high-starch sample and in 37% from low-starch populations. Fifteen wild-born western chimpanzees had 2 diploid AMY1 copies; the human genome reference sequence contains three AMY1 copies.
